name: NVIDIA Corporation
subcategory: GPUs and accelerated computing; CUDA software platform; Nemotron open models
origin_detail: Founded 1993-04-05 in Sunnyvale, California, by Jensen Huang, Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem; IPO 1999-01-22. CUDA, created in 2004 and released in 2007, turned its graphics chips into general-purpose accelerators.
openness_notes: Scored on the AI and developer-platform strategy. Initial 0: proprietary drivers and CUDA ('Whereas Nvidia's CUDA is closed-source, Intel's OneAPI and AMD's ROCm are open source'). Current 1: the core moat (CUDA and user-mode drivers: CUDA, OpenGL, Vulkan) stays closed, while peripheral layers have opened: Linux GPU kernel modules under dual GPL/MIT (May 2022, default from R560 in 2024, required for Grace Hopper and Blackwell), and a large open-model programme (Nemotron) that publishes weights, training data and recipes. The model licence is the non-OSI NVIDIA Open Model License (confirmed for Llama-3.1-Nemotron-Ultra, April 2025; not confirmed from a fetched page for Nemotron 3). Rising toward 2 if Nemotron data and recipes stay open.

license_history.note: Released 2007-02-16; CUDA-enabled GPUs are only available from NVIDIA.
Announced 2022-05-19 with R515; production-ready for Turing/Ampere data-center GPUs; user-mode components stay closed.

license_history.license: Open kernel modules become the default (R560)
license_history.note: Post dated 2024-07-17; open modules required for Grace Hopper and Blackwell.
Released 2025-04-07; Nemotron 3 family (Nano ~30B, Super 100B, Ultra 500B) followed 2025-12-15; NVIDIA describes Nemotron as 'open models with open weights, training data, and recipes'.

relicensing_events.to: Dual GPL/MIT open kernel modules (default from R560, 2024)
relicensing_events.outcome_note: Opened the kernel interface while keeping CUDA and user-space drivers closed.

relicensing_events.to: Large open-weights programme with open data and recipes (Nemotron 3, Dec 2025)
relicensing_events.outcome_note: Weights, training data and technical reports published; licence non-OSI. Strategically, open models drive demand for NVIDIA hardware.

exit_events.note: IPO 1999-01-22; offer valuation not confirmed from a fetched page.

risk_events: 2025-01: lost about $600B of market value in one day (the largest one-day loss for a US company) after DeepSeek showed a cheaper path to frontier-class models
CUDA lock-in invites compatibility layers (HIP, ZLUDA, SCALE) and open rivals (ROCm, oneAPI); ZLUDA was not released officially by AMD or Intel for lack of a business case
2025-12: acquired SchedMD, maker of the open-source Slurm workload manager; NVIDIA stated Slurm would remain open-source and vendor-neutral
Market cap down 8.3% over the year to 2026-11-23 (StockAnalysis)
robustness: Dominant and highly profitable (FY2026 revenue $215.9B with ~42,000 employees). Its moat is a closed software platform (CUDA) on top of its hardware; opening the kernel modules and releasing open models with data strengthens the ecosystem around its chips without opening that moat. Single-vendor control of CUDA is the main structural risk for its customers, not for NVIDIA.
physical_science_relevance: CUDA underpins most GPU-accelerated simulation, molecular dynamics and scientific ML; Earth-2 (open-sourced weather/climate platform, Jan 2026) and Slurm (the standard HPC scheduler) tie NVIDIA directly to physical-science computing.
openness_effect_assessment: Closed CUDA has been the most valuable lock-in in computing: open alternatives (OpenCL, ROCm) exist but CUDA-enabled hardware comes only from NVIDIA. NVIDIA opens what sells more GPUs: kernel modules for data-center Linux, Slurm stewardship, and fully documented open models (Nemotron) that customers train and serve on its hardware. Open models elsewhere cut both ways: DeepSeek's efficient open weights briefly wiped about $600B off its value in January 2025, yet its market cap stood near $4T in November 2026.
key_takeaway: NVIDIA is the complement that profits whenever models are open: the more labs and companies train and run open-weights models, the more GPUs they buy, so NVIDIA now funds one of the most transparent open-model programmes (weights, data, recipes) while keeping CUDA closed. Its openness is therefore strategic and layered: open at the edges and in models, closed at the software platform that locks in its hardware. For the study, NVIDIA shows that a closed platform can coexist with, and benefit from, open science built on top of it.
